title: Short Stuff: Phone Books
summary: A Short Stuff episode on phone books. The hosts describe how white pages and yellow pages were used to find people and businesses, the old habit of calling random people with the same name, and how businesses were listed in categories with the first listing often used by plumbers or florists. They cover the first phone directory in 1878 in New Haven, Connecticut, the thick multi-volume New York City books, and AT&T's profits from Yellow Pages advertising, including the "Let your fingers do the walking" campaign. They explain how the breakup of the Bell monopoly let private companies publish directories, and how directory delivery grew, especially in California. Environmental waste led to recycled paper and Seattle fees for unwanted books. Directory assistance, the 2004 law barring cell numbers from phone books, and the internet reduced Yellow Pages use, though landlines and older adults keep them alive. The episode closes with a host's relative's auto glass shop in Cayuga Falls, Ohio, still advertising in the Yellow Pages.

segments.title: Opening banter on phone books
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the nostalgic topic of phone books and how people used the thick books to find businesses.

segments.title: White pages, yellow pages and looking people up
segments.summary: The white pages listed residents and the yellow pages listed businesses. The hosts joke about finding people by name, calling random namesakes, and the listing order that put one plumber or florist first.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before returning to the history of phone books.

segments.title: Early phone directories and thick New York City books
segments.summary: The first phone directory was published in 1878 in New Haven, Connecticut, with about fifty subscribers on one sheet. Later New York City books came in multiple volumes, and strongmen tore phone books at school assemblies.

segments.title: AT&T profits and Yellow Pages advertising
segments.summary: AT&T earned large sums from Yellow Pages listings, and the phone books were free. Listings were free, but paying to be unlisted was possible. Larger ads brought more notice, and the Let your fingers do the walking campaign promoted the books.
topics: Let your fingers do the walking campaign

segments.title: Bell breakup and rise of competing directories
segments.summary: The breakup of AT&T's monopoly created regional companies and allowed private firms to publish Yellow Pages, increasing the number of directories delivered to homes, including up to ten a year in parts of California in the 1990s.

segments.title: Phone book waste and recycling fees
segments.summary: Phone books created large amounts of paper waste, with about half a billion delivered yearly by 1991. Recycled paper was introduced, and Seattle charged publishers a fee per unwanted book delivered.

segments.title: Decline of phone books
segments.summary: Directory assistance, the internet, and a 2004 Congress law banning cell phone numbers from phone books reduced the books to landline listings.

segments.title: Landlines, older users and Yellow Pages today
segments.summary: Over fifty million US homes still had landlines in 2024, and about ten percent of Americans, and nearly three quarters of those 55 and older, still use Yellow Pages. The episode ends with a plug for Seneco Glass in Cayuga Falls, Ohio.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode with the standard sign-off and production credit.
